title: Uniform projective resolution bound for finite perfect quotients
statement: Let $A$ be a commutative Noetherian ring [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] and $I\subseteq A$ an ideal. For every integer $n\geq1$ put $P_n=A/I^n$, using the ideal powers and quotients of [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient]. Suppose every $P_n$ is finite as a set and its degree-zero complex is perfect [def-pc-perfect-ring-complex]. There is an integer $r\geq0$, independent of $n$, such that every $P_n$ has a resolution by finitely generated projective $A$-modules [def-weil-finitely-generated-module, def-weil-pbc-projective-module] concentrated in cochain degrees $[-r,0]$. Equivalently, for the same $r$, for every $n\geq1$ and every $A$-module $M$, the derived tensor $P_n\otimes_A^{\mathbf L}M$ has cohomology only in degrees $[-r,0]$; here derived tensor is computed by tensoring a projective resolution of $P_n$ with $M$, so $H^{-i}=\operatorname{Tor}_i^A(P_n,M)$ for $i\geq0$ [def-weil-pbc-tor-modules]. The zero quotient is allowed.

source.place: Tag 090V, proposition-Auslander-Buchsbaum: applied to the nonzero finite-length localizations of the perfect quotients. The common-bound conclusion is an agent assembly, not the literal statement of 090V.

proof.text: For each $n$, perfectness supplies a bounded finite projective cochain complex $C_n$ with $H^0(C_n)\cong P_n$ and all other cohomology zero. Remove its positive terms by descending induction on the greatest positive degree $b$ with a nonzero term. Since $H^b(C_n)=0$, the map $C_n^{b-1}\twoheadrightarrow C_n^b$ is surjective and has a section by projectivity of $C_n^b$. Thus $C_n^{b-1}=\ker(d^{b-1})\oplus C_n^b$; the differential from degree $b-2$ lands in the kernel, and the two copies of $C_n^b$ form the contractible identity complex. Delete this summand. The replacement kernel is finite projective: it is a direct summand of a finite projective module, and the images under its projection of a finite generating set generate it. Iterate until all positive terms are zero. The quotient $C_n^0\twoheadrightarrow H^0(C_n)\cong P_n$ then augments an exact finite projective resolution in nonpositive degrees. Denote one such resolution by $Q_n$, of length $s_n\geq0$. Set $r=s_1$. This uses no uniformity yet. If $I=A$, all $P_n=0$ and we may immediately use the zero resolutions with $r=0$.

source.place: Tag 00O4, definition-finite-proj-dim; elementary cancellation of the positive tail of the bounded projective model

proof.text: Fix a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $A$ and write $R=A_{\mathfrak m}$. It is local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak mR$. It is Noetherian: any ideal $J\subseteq R$ is the extension of its contraction $J^c$ (if $a/s\in J$ then $a/1\in J$, and conversely denominators are units); finitely many generators of $J^c$ therefore generate $J$. Localizing $Q_n$ preserves exactness and projectivity, and the images of finite generating sets still generate the localized terms. Hence $(P_n)_{\mathfrak m}$ has finite projective dimension, and $\operatorname{pd}_R((P_1)_{\mathfrak m})\leq r$. If $I\not\subseteq\mathfrak m$, choose $a\in I\setminus\mathfrak m$; the element $a^n$ kills $P_n$ and is invertible after localization, so $(P_n)_{\mathfrak m}=0$ for every $n$.

Now assume $I\subseteq\mathfrak m$ and put $B=(P_1)_{\mathfrak m}$. This is a nonzero cyclic $R$-module: $1/1=0$ would imply that some $u
otin\mathfrak m$ belongs to $I$. Also $B/\mathfrak mRB\cong A/\mathfrak m
e0$, by the map $\overline a/s\mapsto\overline a\,\overline s^{-1}$, whose kernel is $\mathfrak mRB$; thus the depth definition takes its regular-sequence branch. For any $x=a/s\in\mathfrak mR$ take $a\in\mathfrak m$, $s
otin\mathfrak m$. Finiteness of the ring $A/I$ gives $0\leq i<j$ with $\overline a^i=\overline a^j$. The numerator $1-a^{j-i}$ is outside $\mathfrak m$, hence invertible in $R$. The identity $a^i(1-a^{j-i})B=0$ consequently gives $a^iB=0$. Nonzeroness of $B$ excludes $i=0$, and $x$ acts nilpotently on $B$. If multiplication by $x$ were injective, its $i$-fold iterate would be both injective and zero, forcing $B=0$. Therefore no element of $\mathfrak mR$ can start a $B$-regular sequence; the empty sequence is allowed and $\operatorname{depth}_R(B)=0$.

source.place: Tag 00LI, definition-depth; elementary repetition of powers in the finite ring A/I

proof.text: Apply Auslander–Buchsbaum first to the nonzero finite $R$-module $B$: its finite projective dimension was established in step 2, and step 3 gives depth zero. Thus $\operatorname{depth}(R)=\operatorname{pd}_R(B)\leq r$, in particular the ring depth is finite. For each $n$, $(P_n)_{\mathfrak m}$ is likewise cyclic, of finite projective dimension by step 2, and nonzero: $1/1=0$ would give an element outside $\mathfrak m$ lying in $I^n\subseteq\mathfrak m$. The same formula applied to this module gives $\operatorname{pd}_R((P_n)_{\mathfrak m})+\operatorname{depth}_R((P_n)_{\mathfrak m})=\operatorname{depth}(R)\leq r$. Depth is nonnegative by definition, so $\operatorname{pd}_R((P_n)_{\mathfrak m})\leq r$. In conjunction with the zero case of step 2, this bound holds at every maximal ideal, for all $n$.

source.place: Tag 090V, proposition-Auslander-Buchsbaum, applied to the two nonzero finite localized modules

proof.text: Each $P_n$ is cyclic, hence finitely generated over the Noetherian ring $A$. The projective-resolution/Ext characterization turns the bounds of step 4 into $\mathrm{PD}_{\leq r}((P_n)_{\mathfrak m})$ at every maximal ideal (the zero module has the zero resolution). The maximal-localization criterion therefore gives $\mathrm{PD}_{\leq r}(P_n)$ globally. Apply the same characterization in the reverse direction to get a projective resolution of $P_n$ of length at most $r$. The integer $r$ chosen in step 1 depends only on $P_1$, not on $n$.

source.place: Mathlib local-global criterion, ProjectiveDimension.lean:82, and Tag 065R, lemma-projective-dimension-ext

proof.text: Retain the finite projective resolution $Q_n$ of length $s_n$ from step 1. If $s_n\leq r$, pad on the left with zeros. If $s_n>r=0$, step 5 says $P_n$ itself is projective, and its generator $1$ makes it finite, so use $P_n$ in degree zero. If $s_n>r\geq1$, write the resolution in homological degrees and put $K=\ker(Q_{n,r-1}\to Q_{n,r-2})$, with $K=\ker(Q_{n,0}\to P_n)$ when $r=1$. The kernel-projectivity criterion, using step 5 and $e=r-1$, makes $K$ projective. Exactness gives $K=\operatorname{im}(Q_{n,r}\to Q_{n,r-1})$, so the images of finitely many generators of $Q_{n,r}$ generate $K$. Hence $0\to K\to Q_{n,r-1}\to\cdots\to Q_{n,0}\to P_n\to0$ is the required finite projective resolution. Reindexing homological degree $j$ as cochain degree $-j$ yields support in $[-r,0]$.

source.place: Tag 00O5, lemma-independent-resolution; finite-projective shortening as in Tag 0CXE, lemma-what-kind-of-resolutions-Noetherian

proof.text: Tensor the resolution of step 6 with any module $M$ in degree zero. By the definition of Tor and of derived tensor via projective resolutions, its cohomology in degree $-i$ is $\operatorname{Tor}_i^A(P_n,M)$, and its terms vanish outside $[-r,0]$, proving the asserted amplitude. Conversely, if these derived tensors vanish outside $[-r,0]$ for every $M$, then $\operatorname{Tor}_i^A(P_n,M)=0$ for all $i>r$ and all $M$. The finite-module Tor-bound criterion applies because $A$ is Noetherian and $P_n$ is cyclic, and gives $\mathrm{PD}_{\leq r}(P_n)$. The projective-resolution/Ext characterization and the explicit shortening in step 6 recover a resolution by finite projectives of length at most $r$. Thus the two formulations have the same bound, including $r=0$ and zero quotients.

split_report.summary: Proved a common bound r given by the length of a finite projective resolution of A/I, using the elementary depth-zero calculation for finite A/I at supported maximal ideals, the general Auslander–Buchsbaum formula and the Mathlib local-global Ext-bound criterion. Made tensor explicitly derived, removed the unrelated completed sheaf datum from the algebraic statement, and wrote out perfect-model cancellation, localization, shortening and the converse Tor formulation. Two genuinely general ingredients are new: one statement-only formula and one Mathlib leaf.
